reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Rare severe disorder caused by biallelic ETHE1 variants affecting mitochondrial sulphide detoxification
Presents in early infancy with developmental regression, progressive encephalopathy and pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs
Classic triad of associated features: relapsing petechiae/acrocyanosis (orthostatic), chronic diarrhoea, and recurrent vascular/haemorrhagic skin lesions
Biochemical hallmark is persistently elevated ethylmalonic acid in urine, with raised C4 and C5 acylcarnitines and lactic acidaemia
Brain MRI typically shows symmetrical basal ganglia signal change and patchy white-matter lesions
Underlying mechanism is accumulation of hydrogen sulphide, which poisons cytochrome c oxidase and damages the vascular endothelium and gut mucosa
Confirmed by ETHE1 gene sequencing; the metabolic and vascular picture together is highly suggestive
Management is supportive; combined metronidazole (to reduce sulphide-producing gut flora) and N-acetylcysteine has shown some benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Ethylmalonic encephalopathy is caused by loss of function of ETHE1, a mitochondrial matrix sulphur dioxygenase (persulphide dioxygenase) that is essential for the detoxification of hydrogen sulphide generated by gut bacteria and endogenous metabolism. When ETHE1 activity is lost, hydrogen sulphide accumulates in tissues where it inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) of the respiratory chain and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. This produces a mitochondrial energy-failure state with lactic acidosis, accumulation of ethylmalonic acid and short-chain acylcarnitines, and toxic injury to the highly perfused brain, gastrointestinal mucosa and vascular endothelium, accounting for the encephalopathy, chronic diarrhoea and relapsing petechial/vascular skin lesions. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (also raises ethylmalonic acid)
Mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders including Leigh syndrome
Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type II)
Other causes of infantile lactic acidosis
Vasculitic or coagulopathic causes of petechiae and acrocyanosis
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids demonstrating persistent ethylmalonic aciduria
Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised C4 butyryl and C5 species)
Brain MRI for symmetrical basal ganglia and white-matter changes
Thiosulphate measurement as a marker of sulphide accumulation where available
Assessment of coagulation and platelet function given vascular lesions
redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with developmental regression
Recurrent haemorrhagic/petechial skin lesions and acrocyanosis
Severe lactic acidosis during intercurrent illness
Refractory chronic diarrhoea with failure to thrive
Neurological deterioration with new basal ganglia lesions
reference.prognosis: The disorder is typically severe and progressive with early death in classic cases, although combined metronidazole and N-acetylcysteine therapy may slow progression in some patients; overall prognosis remains guarded.
pitfalls: Attributing ethylmalonic aciduria solely to short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency and missing ETHE1 disease
Interpreting the petechiae as a primary bleeding or vasculitic disorder
Overlooking the diagnostic value of combining the metabolic and vascular/gastrointestinal features
Delaying targeted therapy while pursuing an extensive alternative workup
Assuming a purely mitochondrial cocktail will help without addressing sulphide toxicity
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
